title: SRLAgent: Enhancing Self-Regulated Learning Skills through Gamification and LLM Assistance
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how to improve self-regulated learning (SRL) skills among college students, especially freshmen who struggle with goal-setting, time management, maintaining study routines, and reflection. The authors argue that existing SRL interventions and educational technologies often provide static support, limited personalization, and insufficient engagement. To better understand student needs, they first conducted a formative mixed-methods study with 59 university students using surveys and semi-structured interviews.

Based on these findings, the authors developed SRLAgent, a gamified Minecraft-based learning environment augmented with large language model (LLM) support. The system is grounded in Zimmerman’s three-phase SRL model—forethought, performance, and reflection—and includes planning support, real-time monitoring, specialized tutoring agents, and reflection prompts. Students interact with learning materials, quizzes, writing tasks, and conversational AI agents within a virtual campus environment. The system is designed to scaffold goal-setting, strategic learning, time management, and reflective practice while maintaining engagement through game mechanics.

The empirical evaluation used a between-subjects experiment with 45 Chinese college freshmen at a university in China. Participants were randomly assigned to one of three conditions: traditional multimedia learning, a baseline Minecraft SRLAgent version without SRL-specific features, or the full SRLAgent system. The intervention focused on learning about LLM agents in a one-hour lab study including pretest, tutorial, learning session, and post-test. Outcomes included self-regulated learning skills, knowledge test performance, engagement, and trust in AI.

The main findings indicate that the full SRLAgent condition produced a significant pre-post improvement in self-reported SRL skills, whereas the other two conditions did not. However, learning outcome gains on the knowledge test did not significantly differ between SRLAgent and the baseline system without SRL features. Engagement and trust in AI showed descriptive trends favoring SRLAgent, but these differences were not statistically significant. Overall, the paper concludes that embedding SRL scaffolding and real-time LLM assistance in a gamified environment can strengthen students’ self-regulation, though stronger evidence is still needed for effects on content learning, engagement, and trust.

identified_tools.name: SRLAgent
identified_tools.description: An LLM-assisted, Minecraft-based gamified learning system designed to support self-regulated learning through planning, monitoring, tutoring, and reflection agents.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as a college learning environment for teaching the concept of 'LLM agents' while scaffolding self-regulated learning via goal-setting, real-time feedback, time management, and reflection features.

findings.finding_summary: In the SRLAgent condition, self-regulated learning scores increased significantly from pretest (M=5.66, SD=.67) to post-test (M=5.92, SD=.65), with t(15)=4.41, p<.001, Cohen’s d=.234. No significant pre-post SRL gains were observed in the SRLAgent-without-SRL-features group or the multimedia learning group.
findings.measure: Academic Self-Regulated Learning Questionnaire (18-item ASLQ-derived SRL score, 7-point Likert scale)

findings.finding_summary: For learning outcomes on LLM agent content, the SRLAgent group showed descriptive pre-post gains (M diff=1.69, SD=1.40), but post-intervention performance did not differ significantly from the SRLAgent-without-SRL-features group, t(28)=1.59, p=.123. All groups showed gains, with the largest descriptive improvement in the SRLAgent-without-SRL-features group (M diff=2.53, SD=2.56).
findings.measure: 12-item Hugging Face LLM Agent tutorial final test (multiple-choice knowledge test)

findings.finding_summary: Participants using SRLAgent reported higher average engagement scores (M=4.17, SD=.45) than those using the baseline SRLAgent without SRL features (M=3.80, SD=.82), but the difference was not statistically significant, t(28)=1.59, p=.123. The paper interprets this as a descriptive trend suggesting potentially higher engagement with SRL scaffolding and adaptive feedback.
findings.measure: User Engagement Scale (UES), 30-item post-test engagement score

findings.finding_summary: Within the SRLAgent group, trust in the AI system increased modestly from pretest (M=4.66, SD=.73) to post-test (M=4.91, SD=.80), but this change was not statistically significant, t(15)=1.62, p=.127. A one-way ANOVA on post-test trust across conditions was also non-significant, F(2,42)=1.21, p=.310, though descriptive means favored SRLAgent over multimedia learning and SRLAgent without SRL features.
findings.measure: 12-item Jian Trust Scale adapted for AI systems

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical between-subjects randomized comparison with pre/post measurement and two baselines, which is stronger than descriptive or correlational work. However, the sample is small (N=45 total) and reported evidence is limited to a single short-duration study in higher education, so some concerns remain.
impact_tier_rationale: The strongest reported effect is a statistically significant positive improvement in SRL skills for SRLAgent with Cohen’s d=0.234, which meets the medium-impact threshold used here. Other outcomes were descriptive or non-significant, so overall impact is positive but modest and somewhat mixed.
